title: Muḍāriʻ Verbs in the Quran, Ẓurūf (Adverbs of Time/Place), and the Pattern of Ism al-Ẓarf
summary: The session began with students sharing homework sentences using previously learned vocabulary and Quranic examples of مُضَارِع (muḍāriʻ) verbs, with the teacher providing corrections and contextual explanations. The class then continued reading a textbook passage (page 69) about a man's daily routine, through which the teacher introduced and reinforced several ظُرُوف (ẓurūf — adverbs of time and place), including دَائِمًا، أَحْيَانًا، مَرَّةً أُخْرَى، and مُتَأَخِّرًا. The teacher also explained the grammatical pattern of اسم الظرف (ism al-ẓarf), showing how verb roots produce words indicating a place or time of action, with examples such as مَصْنَع، مَكْتَب، مَدْرَسَة، and مَسْجِد.
key_points: The مُضَارِع (muḍāriʻ) verb serves double duty: it expresses both present continuous action ('he is doing it right now') and habitual action ('he does it regularly'). Context determines which meaning applies. For example, يَذْهَبُ إِلَى السُّوقِ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ means 'he goes to the market every day' — a habit, not a single ongoing action. This dual function is central to reading the lesson's passage correctly.

ظَرْف (ẓarf) is an adverb of time or place. A critical grammatical rule is that ظُرُوف (adverbs) take فَتْحَة. This explains why دَائِمًا (always), أَحْيَانًا (sometimes), مَرَّةً أُخْرَى (again/another time), مُتَأَخِّرًا (late), مُبَكِّرًا (early), and كُلَّ يَوْمٍ (every day) all end in فَتْحَة. Recognizing a word as a ظَرْف immediately tells you its grammatical ending.

كُلُّ (kullu — every/all) is almost always مُضَاف (in an annexation construction) to the word after it, which means the word after كُلُّ takes كَسْرَة. Crucially, the word after كُلُّ must be singular — not plural. So كُلَّ يَوْمٍ (every day) is correct; كُلَّ أَيَّامٍ is a beginner error. When كُلُّ itself functions as a ظَرْف, it takes فَتْحَة (كُلَّ يَوْمٍ). When it is the مَفْعُول (object) of a verb, it also takes فَتْحَة for that reason instead.

اسم الظرف (ism al-ẓarf) is a noun derived from a verb root using the pattern مَفْعَل or مَفْعِل. It names the place or time of the action described by that root. Knowing this pattern unlocks the meaning of countless Arabic words: صَنَعَ (to make) → مَصْنَع (factory); كَتَبَ (to write) → مَكْتَب (office/desk); دَرَسَ (to study) → مَدْرَسَة (school); سَجَدَ (to prostrate) → مَسْجِد (mosque); ذَهَبَ (to go) → مَذْهَب (path/school of thought); زَارَ (to visit) → مَزَار (place of visitation); قَبَرَ (to bury) → مَقْبَرَة (graveyard). Unlike a regular ظَرْف, an اسم الظرف does not automatically take فَتْحَة.

بَعْدَ (after) is a ظَرْف that is always مُضَاف to the word following it, so the word after بَعْدَ takes كَسْرَة — e.g., بَعْدَ صَلَاةِ الْفَجْرِ (after Fajr prayer). It must not be confused with بُعْد (distance/farness), which is a completely different word — e.g., عَلَى بُعْدِ ثَلَاثَةِ أَمْيَالٍ (at a distance of three miles). The difference is in the vowel on the ب.

عَادَ (ʻāda) and أَعَادَ (aʻāda) are two distinct verbs that must not be confused. عَادَ means the subject themselves returns (intransitive). أَعَادَ يُعِيدُ means to return or bring something back (transitive — requires an object). Allah uses أَعَادَ in كَمَا بَدَأْنَا أَوَّلَ خَلْقٍ نُعِيدُ to indicate bringing creation back to life — not عَادَ — because there is a direct object (creation being returned).

خَلَقَ has two distinct meanings that carry different theological implications: (1) to create from nothing (ex nihilo) — exclusive to Allah; (2) to fashion or shape something (تَصْوِير) — which can apply to others, as Allah Himself used it for ʻĪsā (A.S.) in أَنِّي أَخْلُقُ لَكُمْ مِنَ الطِّينِ كَهَيْئَةِ الطَّيْرِ. Knowing this distinction prevents misunderstanding Quranic verses and avoids incorrectly correcting others.

The مُضَارِع verbs identified from the Quran in this lesson — يَعْمَلُونَ (they do), يَخْشَى / يَخْشَوْنَ (he/they fear), يَذُوقُونَ (they taste), يَذْكُرُونَ (they remember), يَمْنَعُونَ (they prevent), يَحْزَنُونَ (they are sad) — all follow the same core مُضَارِع pattern for third-person plural masculine (يَفْعَلُونَ). The teacher noted that صِيغَةُ الْمَجْهُول (passive voice, e.g., قُتِلَ — 'he was killed') looks similar but is a separate form to be studied later; students should not confuse it with the active مُضَارِع.

Arabic root letters are the key to understanding the language mathematically. Once you know a three-letter root and its core meaning, you can derive and understand a large number of related words. For example, from ذَهَبَ (to go): يَذْهَبُ (he goes), مَذْهَب (school of thought/path). From عَمِلَ (to work): يَعْمَلُ (he works), عَامِل (worker — اسم الفاعل), مَعْمَل (laboratory/workshop — اسم الظرف). The teacher emphasized this as the core beauty and logic of Arabic.

فَعَلَ (to do) and عَمِلَ (to work/do) are not interchangeable. فَعَلَ is the most generic, vague verb in Arabic — it simply means 'to do something' with no specific connotation. عَمِلَ carries the more specific meaning of performing work or labor. Use فَعَلَ when asking 'what did he do?' in a general sense; use عَمِلَ when the context involves actual work or effort.
questions: [00:02:01] Q: Is خَلَقَ only used for Allah? — A: خَلَقَ has multiple meanings. If used in the sense of creating from nothing (bringing something into existence from non-existence), then yes, that is exclusive to Allah. However, خَلَقَ can also mean to fashion or shape something (تَصْوِير), and in that sense it can be used for others — Allah Himself used it for ʻĪsā (A.S.) in the Quran: أَنِّي أَخْلُقُ لَكُمْ مِنَ الطِّينِ كَهَيْئَةِ الطَّيْرِ. Technically it is permissible to use it in a different context, but it is no longer commonly used for anyone besides Allah.

[00:06:00] Q: Does عَادَ mean to return an object to someone, or a person returning themselves? — A: عَادَ is only used in the sense of a person (or thing) themselves returning. To return something to someone else, you use the different verb أَعَادَ يُعِيدُ, which is why Allah uses that verb to indicate bringing us back to life.

[00:16:00] Q: Is لَا يَسْمَعُونَ a مُضَارِع (present tense) verb? — A: The teacher clarified that لَا يَسْمَعُونَ in that context is صِيغَةُ النَّهْي (a prohibitive command — 'do not'), not a مُضَارِع used for present or future tense.

[00:27:00] Q: Why does كُلَّ in the Quran sometimes have فَتْحَة instead of ضَمَّة? — A: In that Quranic instance, كُلَّ is the مَفْعُول (object) of the verb, so it takes فَتْحَة. The example given was وَكُلَّ إِنسَانٍ أَلْزَمْنَاهُ, which is equivalent in meaning to أَلْزَمْنَا كُلَّ إِنسَانٍ طَائِرَهُ.

[00:28:00] Q: Why is the surah called both Surah Bani Isra'il and Surah al-Isra'? — A: They are simply two different names for the same surah. Many surahs have multiple names — for example, Surah al-Fatiha has been mentioned with around 20 names by some scholars.

[00:44:00] Q: What is the difference between عَمِلَ and فَعَلَ? — A: فَعَلَ is the most generic word in Arabic meaning 'to do something' — it is very vague. عَمِلَ is similar but carries more the specific meaning of work or labor. So فَعَلَ is used when asking 'what did he do?' in a general sense, while عَمِلَ leans toward actual work.

[00:47:00] Q: Was مُتَأَخِّرًا already learned? — A: No, it had not been covered yet. The teacher introduced it here, explaining it means 'late' and is a ظَرْف (hence فَتْحَة). He also introduced its opposite مُبَكِّرًا (early), noting that the root بُكْرَة literally means the early part of the morning, as in the Quranic وَسَبِّحُوا بُكْرَةً وَأَصِيلًا, though مُبَكِّرًا is used generally for 'early' and not restricted to the morning.

quiz.q: What does مَزَار mean and what is its root verb?
options: A farm; from زَرَعَ (to plant)
A place of visitation; from زَارَ (to visit)
A marketplace; from زَادَ (to increase)
A storage place; from خَزَنَ (to store)
quiz.a: The teacher explained that زَارَ يَزُورُ means to visit, and مَزَار — following the اسم الظرف pattern — means a place that is visited. The teacher noted this is the literal meaning of the word.

quiz.q: What does أَحْيَانًا mean, and what word is it technically the plural of?
options: It means 'always' and is the plural of دَوَام
It means 'sometimes' and is the plural of حِين (a time/moment)
It means 'again' and is the plural of مَرَّة
It means 'late' and is the plural of تَأَخُّر
quiz.a: أَحْيَانًا means 'sometimes.' The teacher explained it is technically the plural of حِين, which means a time or moment. As a ظَرْف, it takes فَتْحَة.

quiz.q: What does مَرَّةً أُخْرَى mean, and why does it take فَتْحَة?
options: It means 'the first time' and takes فَتْحَة because it is مُبْتَدَأ
It means 'another time / again' and takes فَتْحَة because it is a ظَرْف
It means 'a second time' and takes فَتْحَة because it is مُضَاف إِلَيْه
It means 'every time' and takes فَتْحَة because it is مَفْعُول بِهِ
quiz.a: مَرَّةً أُخْرَى means 'another time' or 'again.' The teacher explained it is a ظَرْف, which is why it takes فَتْحَة. He gave the example of people saying مَرَّةً أُخْرَى to a reciter, meaning 'do it again.'

quiz.q: According to the teacher, what is the difference between مَرَّةً أُخْرَى and مَرَّةً ثَانِيَةً?
options: مَرَّةً أُخْرَى means again; مَرَّةً ثَانِيَةً means for the last time
مَرَّةً أُخْرَى means another time; مَرَّةً ثَانِيَةً means a second time — pretty much the same meaning
مَرَّةً أُخْرَى means sometimes; مَرَّةً ثَانِيَةً means always
مَرَّةً أُخْرَى is used only in the Quran; مَرَّةً ثَانِيَةً is used only in everyday speech
quiz.a: The teacher explained that مَرَّةً أُخْرَى means 'another time' and مَرَّةً ثَانِيَةً means 'a second time,' and that they are pretty much the same in meaning.

quiz.q: What does مُتَأَخِّرًا mean, and what is its opposite as introduced in the lesson?
options: مُتَأَخِّرًا means early; its opposite is مُبَكِّرًا meaning late
مُتَأَخِّرًا means late; its opposite is مُبَكِّرًا meaning early
مُتَأَخِّرًا means always; its opposite is أَحْيَانًا meaning sometimes
مُتَأَخِّرًا means again; its opposite is دَائِمًا meaning always
quiz.a: مُتَأَخِّرًا means 'late' and its opposite is مُبَكِّرًا meaning 'early.' Both are ظُرُوف and take فَتْحَة. The teacher gave the examples: جَاءَ الطَّالِبُ مُبَكِّرًا إِلَى الدَّرْسِ (the student came to class early) and جَاءَ الطَّالِبُ إِلَى الدَّرْسِ مُتَأَخِّرًا (the student came to class late).

quiz.q: What is the literal root meaning of بُكْرَة, from which مُبَكِّرًا is derived?
options: The late evening
The early morning
The middle of the day
The time just before sunset
quiz.a: The teacher explained that بُكْرَة literally means the early part of the morning, as in the Quranic وَسَبِّحُوا بُكْرَةً وَأَصِيلًا. However, مُبَكِّرًا is used generally to mean 'early' and is not restricted to the morning.

quiz.q: What is the grammatical relationship between بَعْدَ and the word that follows it?
options: بَعْدَ is a فِعْل and the word after it is its فَاعِل, taking ضَمَّة
بَعْدَ is a ظَرْف and is مُضَاف to the word after it, so the word after it takes كَسْرَة
بَعْدَ is a حَرْف جَرّ and causes the word after it to take كَسْرَة
بَعْدَ is مُبْتَدَأ and the word after it is its خَبَر, taking ضَمَّة
quiz.a: The teacher explained that بَعْدَ is a ظَرْف and is مُضَاف to the word that follows it, meaning the word after بَعْدَ takes كَسْرَة as the مُضَاف إِلَيْه. The Quranic example given was وَمِنْ بَعْدِ صَلَاةِ الْعِشَاءِ.

quiz.q: What is the difference between بَعْدَ and بُعْد as explained in the lesson?
options: بَعْدَ means distance; بُعْد means after
بَعْدَ means after; بُعْد means distance or farness
They are the same word with different spellings
بَعْدَ is used only in the Quran; بُعْد is used only in everyday speech
quiz.a: The teacher distinguished between the two: بَعْدَ means 'after' (a ظَرْف of time), while بُعْد means distance or farness. The example given for بُعْد was هَذَا الْبَيْتُ عَلَى بُعْدِ ثَلَاثَةِ أَمْيَالٍ — 'this house is at a distance of three miles.'

quiz.q: What are the two meanings the مُضَارِع verb يَذْهَبُ can carry, as explained by the teacher?
options: He went (past) and he will go (future)
He is going right now (present continuous) and he goes habitually (general habit)
He went (past) and he is going (present continuous)
He goes (habit) and he went (past)
quiz.a: The teacher explained that يَذْهَبُ can mean 'he is going' (present continuous, right now) or 'he goes' (a habitual action). In the lesson's reading passage, it is used in the habitual sense — 'he always goes to the market after Fajr.'

quiz.q: The مُضَارِع verb يَخْشَى was identified from the Quran. What does it mean, and in which Quranic contexts did the teacher mention it?
options: To remember; mentioned in the context of those who remember Allah standing and sitting
To fear; mentioned in the verse about only the scholars truly fearing Allah, and in the verse about Musa speaking softly to Firaun
To taste; mentioned in the context of Jahannam
To prevent; mentioned in the context of Surah Ma'oon
quiz.a: يَخْشَى means to fear. The teacher mentioned two Quranic contexts: (1) the verse stating that only the scholars (عُلَمَاء) from among Allah's slaves truly fear Him, and (2) the verse فَقُولَا لَهُ قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا لَعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أَوْ يَخْشَى, where Allah instructs Musa (A.S.) to speak softly to Firaun so that he may take heed or fear.

quiz.q: The مُضَارِع verb يَمْنَعُونَ was identified from Surah Ma'oon. What does it mean in that context?
options: They remember; referring to those who remember Allah constantly
They prevent; referring to those who are so stingy they refuse even the smallest help to others
They taste; referring to those who will taste punishment
They fear; referring to those who fear the Day of Judgment
quiz.a: يَمْنَعُونَ means 'they prevent.' The teacher explained that in Surah Ma'oon, it refers to those who are so stingy (بَخِيل) — because they do not believe in the hereafter or its rewards — that they refuse even the smallest form of help (مَاعُون) to others.

quiz.q: The مُضَارِع verb يَذُوقُونَ was identified from the Quran. What does it mean and in what context was it mentioned?
options: They hear; mentioned in the context of those who listen to the Quran
They taste; mentioned in the context of Jahannam — they will not taste coolness or drink in it
They remember; mentioned in the context of those who remember Allah
They see; mentioned in the context of those who witness the truth
quiz.a: يَذُوقُونَ means 'they taste,' from the root ذَاقَ (past tense). The teacher mentioned it in the context of Jahannam: لَا يَذُوقُونَ فِيهَا بَرْدًا وَلَا شَرَابًا — they will not taste in it any coolness or drink.

quiz.q: What does يَحْزَنُونَ mean, and what is the root noun related to it mentioned in the lesson?
options: They are angry; related to the noun غَضَب (anger)
They are sad; related to the noun حُزْن (sadness)
They are afraid; related to the noun خَوْف (fear)
They are patient; related to the noun صَبْر (patience)
quiz.a: يَحْزَنُونَ means 'they are sad' or 'they experience sadness.' The teacher mentioned that حَزِنَ is the past tense and حُزْن is the noun meaning sadness. The verse cited was فَلَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ.

quiz.q: What is صِيغَةُ الْمَجْهُول, and how did the teacher treat it in this lesson?
options: It is the plural form of the مُضَارِع verb; the teacher taught it fully in this lesson
It is the passive voice form where the doer is not mentioned; the teacher acknowledged it but said it will be covered in a future lesson
It is the command form of the verb; the teacher said it is the same as the مُضَارِع
It is the dual form of the verb; the teacher said students should already know it
quiz.a: صِيغَةُ الْمَجْهُول is the passive voice, where the doer of the action is not mentioned — for example, قُتِلَ هَذَا الشَّخْصُ (such and such person was killed). The teacher acknowledged a student's Quranic example that used this form but clarified it is a slightly different verb form that will be taught in a future lesson.

quiz.q: What is the difference between عَمِلَ and فَعَلَ according to the teacher?
options: فَعَلَ specifically means to work; عَمِلَ is the generic word for doing anything
فَعَلَ is the most generic word meaning 'to do something'; عَمِلَ carries more the specific meaning of work or labor
They are completely synonymous and interchangeable in all contexts
فَعَلَ is used only in the past tense; عَمِلَ is used only in the present tense
quiz.a: The teacher explained that فَعَلَ is the most generic, vague word in Arabic meaning 'to do something,' while عَمِلَ is similar but leans more toward the meaning of actual work or labor. فَعَلَ is used when asking 'what did he do?' in a general sense.

quiz.q: How do you say 8:45 in Arabic, as explained in the lesson?
options: الثَّامِنَةُ وَخَمْسَةٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ دَقِيقَةً
التَّاسِعَةُ إِلَّا رُبْعًا
الثَّامِنَةُ وَالنِّصْفُ
التَّاسِعَةُ وَالرُّبْعُ
quiz.a: 8:45 is expressed as التَّاسِعَةُ إِلَّا رُبْعًا — literally 'the ninth (hour) except a quarter,' meaning nine o'clock minus a quarter, which equals 8:45.

quiz.q: What does نِصْف mean, and in what context was it mentioned in the lesson?
options: A quarter; mentioned when discussing how to say 8:15
Half; mentioned when discussing how to say 1:30 (الْوَاحِدَةُ وَنِصْف)
A third; mentioned when discussing how to divide the hours
Two-thirds; mentioned when discussing prayer times
quiz.a: نِصْف means 'half.' The teacher mentioned it in the context of telling time, specifically when the reading passage mentioned الْوَاحِدَةُ وَنِصْف to mean 1:30. The teacher noted these time expressions had been learned previously.

quiz.q: What does دَائِمًا mean, and is it a ظَرْف?
options: It means 'sometimes' and is not a ظَرْف
It means 'always' and yes, it is a ظَرْف
It means 'again' and is a ظَرْف
It means 'early' and is not a ظَرْف
quiz.a: دَائِمًا means 'always' and it is indeed a ظَرْف (adverb of time), which is why it takes فَتْحَة. The teacher confirmed this when a student asked, and noted that both دَائِمًا and أَحْيَانًا are ظُرُوف.

quiz.q: What does the word صُحُف mean in the lesson's reading passage, and what is its singular form?
options: Books; singular is كِتَاب
Newspapers; singular is صَحِيفَة
Letters; singular is رِسَالَة
Magazines; singular is مَجَلَّة
quiz.a: The teacher explained that صُحُف is the plural of صَحِيفَة, meaning newspaper. In the reading passage, the character reads newspapers (يَقْرَأُ الصُّحُفَ) and listens to the news on the radio.

quiz.q: In the reading passage, the word عَامِل was used. What does it mean and what grammatical category does it belong to?
options: A manager; it is an اسم الظرف
A worker or employee; it is an اسم الفاعل (the doer of the action)
A factory; it is an اسم الظرف
An engineer; it is an اسم المفعول
quiz.a: عَامِل means a worker or employee. The teacher explained it is an اسم الفاعل — a word indicating the doer of the action — derived from عَمِلَ (to work). The teacher reminded students they had previously learned the concept of اسم الفاعل.

quiz.q: According to the teacher, what is the key grammatical difference between a regular ظَرْف and an اسم الظرف in terms of their endings?
options: A regular ظَرْف takes كَسْرَة; an اسم الظرف takes ضَمَّة
A regular ظَرْف generally takes فَتْحَة; an اسم الظرف does not have that same quality
They both always take فَتْحَة with no difference
A regular ظَرْف takes ضَمَّة; an اسم الظرف takes فَتْحَة
quiz.a: The teacher pointed out that a regular ظَرْف generally takes فَتْحَة, but an اسم الظرف does not have that same quality. He told students to keep this distinction in mind.

quiz.q: The teacher explained the word مَدْرَسَة as an اسم الظرف. What is its root verb and what does the اسم الظرف literally mean?
options: Root: دَرَّسَ (to teach); literally means the person who teaches
Root: دَرَسَ (to study); literally means the place where one studies
Root: دَرَسَ (to study); literally means the act of studying
Root: دَرَّسَ (to teach); literally means the place where teaching is done exclusively by scholars
quiz.a: The teacher explained that دَرَسَ means to study, and مَدْرَسَة — following the اسم الظرف pattern — means the place where one studies, i.e., a school or madrasa.

quiz.q: How many ظُرُوف did the teacher count as having been introduced in this lesson's reading passage?
options: Three: دَائِمًا، أَحْيَانًا، مُتَأَخِّرًا
Four or five: دَائِمًا، أَحْيَانًا، مَرَّةً أُخْرَى، مُتَأَخِّرًا, and possibly كُلَّ يَوْمٍ
Two: دَائِمًا and أَحْيَانًا only
Six: including مُبَكِّرًا، بَعْدَ، and قَبْلَ as well
quiz.a: The teacher counted four ظُرُوف — دَائِمًا، أَحْيَانًا، مَرَّةً أُخْرَى، مُتَأَخِّرًا — and then said if you count كُلَّ يَوْمٍ, that makes five. He highlighted this as a focus of the lesson.

quiz.q: What homework exercises did the teacher assign at the end of the lesson?
options: Only exercise one: answer questions based on the reading passage
Exercises one, four, and five: answer comprehension questions, write the مُضَارِع of given verbs, and fill in blanks with the correct مُضَارِع verb
Exercises two and three only: correct sentences and translate a passage
Find ten مُضَارِع verbs from the Quran and write their meanings
quiz.a: The teacher assigned exercises one, four, and five. Exercise one involves answering comprehension questions based on the reading passage. Exercise four asks students to write the مُضَارِع form of given past tense verbs (e.g., كَتَبَ → يَكْتُبُ). Exercise five is a fill-in-the-blank exercise using the correct مُضَارِع verb.

quiz.q: According to the teacher, what does the word مَذْهَب literally mean based on its root, and how is that meaning connected to its usage in Islamic scholarship?
options: It literally means a place of writing, and it is used for schools of thought because scholars write their rulings
It literally means a path or the place where one goes, and it is used for schools of jurisprudence as if a person takes that path to follow the deen
It literally means a place of gathering, and it is used because scholars gather to discuss rulings
It literally means a place of returning, and it is used because students return to these schools repeatedly
quiz.a: The teacher explained that ذَهَبَ means to go, so مَذْهَب literally means a path — the place where one goes. It is used for schools of Islamic jurisprudence because it is as if a person takes that path to follow the deen. The teacher used this as an example of the beauty of the Arabic language and how knowing root meanings unlocks understanding.

quiz.q: Why is understanding Arabic root letters so important according to the teacher?
options: Because root letters determine whether a word is masculine or feminine
Because once you know the meaning of a three-letter root, you can understand a large number of derived words and forms
Because root letters tell you which grammatical case a word takes
Because root letters are only relevant for Quranic vocabulary, not everyday Arabic
quiz.a: The teacher emphasized that Arabic is a mathematical language — once you know the core meaning of a three-letter root, you can derive and understand an almost endless number of related words. For example, knowing ذَهَبَ (to go) gives you يَذْهَبُ, مَذْهَب, and other forms. This is why the teacher recommended the book shared in the group that teaches root words.

quiz.q: Which of the following مُضَارِع verbs from the Quran means 'they remember,' and what is its past tense root?
options: يَخْشَوْنَ; root is خَشِيَ
يَذْكُرُونَ; root is ذَكَرَ
يَمْنَعُونَ; root is مَنَعَ
يَحْزَنُونَ; root is حَزِنَ
quiz.a: يَذْكُرُونَ means 'they remember' and its past tense root is ذَكَرَ. The teacher mentioned the Quranic verse about remembering Allah standing, sitting, and lying on one's sides as the context for this verb.

quiz.q: The مُضَارِع verb يَعْمَلُونَ was identified from the Quran. What does it mean and what person, number, and gender does it represent?
options: He does; third person singular masculine
They do; third person plural masculine
You all do; second person plural masculine
We do; first person plural
quiz.a: يَعْمَلُونَ means 'they do' and represents the third person plural masculine form of the مُضَارِع. The teacher confirmed this when a student brought it as a Quranic example, noting it means 'they are doing' or 'they do good deeds.'

quiz.q: The مُضَارِع verb قَرَأَ becomes يَقْرَأُ in the present tense. In the reading passage, what does the character read?
options: Books from the library
Newspapers (الصُّحُفَ)
Letters from his family
Reports from the factory
quiz.a: In the reading passage, the character يَقْرَأُ الصُّحُفَ — he reads newspapers. The teacher noted that صُحُف is the plural of صَحِيفَة (newspaper), and that يَقْرَأُ is the مُضَارِع form of قَرَأَ (to read), consistent with the lesson's focus on present tense verbs.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what is مَصْنَع and what verb root does it come from?
options: A library; from كَتَبَ (to write)
A factory; from صَنَعَ (to make/manufacture)
A school; from دَرَسَ (to study)
A marketplace; from بَاعَ (to sell)
quiz.a: مَصْنَع means a factory and comes from the root صَنَعَ (to make or manufacture). It follows the اسم الظرف pattern مَفْعَل, indicating the place where the action of making/manufacturing takes place. The reading passage in this lesson is set around a character who goes to his مَصْنَع.
